entities.name: Second Persian invasion of Greece
entities.label: EventWindow
entities.summary:
The Second Persian invasion of Greece was a pivotal event in world history, marking a significant turning point in the Greco-Persian Wars. In 479 BCE, the combined forces of the Hellenic League, led by the Spartans, defeated the Persian army at the Battle of Plataea, ultimately repelling the Persian invasion and securing Greek independence.

This invasion was a culmination of the Persian Empire's expansion under King Xerxes I, who sought to conquer all of Greece. The invasion force, estimated to be around 100,000 soldiers, was met with fierce resistance from the Greeks, who were determined to defend their cities and way of life. The Persian army's defeat at Plataea marked a decisive shift in the balance of power between the East and the West.

The legacy of the Second Persian invasion of Greece can be seen in the subsequent rise of Athens and Sparta, two city-states that would go on to play a significant role in shaping Western civilization. The defeat of the Persians also paved the way for the development of democracy in ancient Greece, which would influence the course of Western politics for centuries to come.

As the Greek historian Herodotus noted, 'The battle of Plataea was a turning point in the war, for it marked the beginning of the end of the Persian Empire's expansion.' The Second Persian invasion of Greece may have been a localized event, but its impact on world history was profound.
